cards.title: Is the Shannon capacity of a finite graph computable?
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A such that, for every finite simple undirected graph G and every integer k≥1, A on input (G,k) halts and outputs integers a and b>0 with |a/b−Θ(G)|≤2^(−k)? No bound on running time is imposed.
cards.why: Asks whether a finite zero-error communication model has an effectively approximable asymptotic information rate.

progress.text: Alon–Lubetzky demonstrate large later increases beyond arbitrarily long fixed prefixes of the independence series.
A primary paper on spectral bounds explicitly states that general Shannon capacity is not known to be computable.
New special-family values and connected examples of finite-power nonattainment are published; they do not decide general effective approximation.

cards.definitions: Encode G with vertices {1,…,n}, n≥0, by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal n×n binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For m≥1, the strong power G^⊠m has vertex set {1,…,n}^m. Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either x_j=y_j or {x_j,y_j} is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; α(H) is its maximum cardinality, with α of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define Θ(G)=sup_{m≥1} α(G^⊠m)^(1/m). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as m→∞, and 1≤Θ(G)≤n; set Θ(G)=0 when n=0. The desired output approximates Θ itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.

context_blocks.title: Zero-error communication as a graph
context_blocks.text: Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

context_blocks.title: Why longer blocks matter
context_blocks.text: A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity √5. For nonempty graphs, log₂Θ(G) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

context_blocks.title: A limit needs an effective error guarantee
context_blocks.text: Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

context_blocks.title: Recent progress and the scope of the question
context_blocks.text: The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of C₇ is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

sentences: A graph records which transmitted symbols can be confused.
Its Shannon capacity is the limiting number of distinguishable messages per use when arbitrarily long blocks are allowed.
The question asks for one terminating algorithm that approximates this quantity to any requested absolute accuracy on every finite graph.
Known examples show that fixed finite prefixes and finite-power attainment do not supply a general stopping guarantee.
The target concerns computability itself, with no required running-time bound.

cards.context:
Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity √5. For nonempty graphs, log₂Θ(G) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of C₇ is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
